claim: Shantideva was a famous 8th-century Indian Buddhist monk
evidence: Shantideva was an 8th-century CE Indian philosopher, Buddhist monk, poet and scholar at Nalanda.

claim: Sakya Pandita brought Sakya teachings to the Ming emperor's court
evidence: Sakya Pandita (1182-1251) taught Godan Khan (Mongol) at Liangzhou c.1247, in the Mongol/Yuan era; the Ming began 1368.
correction: Sakya Pandita (1182-1251) was summoned by the Mongol prince Godan Khan, not a Ming emperor (Ming founded 1368).

claim: The syllables are a transliteration of the Sanskrit Vajrasattva mantra
evidence: The text ('badzra sa tva sa ma ya... ha ha ha ha ho bhagavan sarva tathagata badzra ma me muntsa...') matches the closing of the Vajrasattva hundred-syllable mantra (Sanskrit: ...hum ha ha ha ha hoh bhagavan sarvatathagatavajra ma me muncha vajribhava mahasamayasattva ah).

evidence: Panacanantarya: patricide, matricide, killing an arhat, wounding a buddha, causing a schism in the sangha.

evidence: Tirthika denotes non-Buddhist teachers/followers such as the six heretical teachers; Tibetan mu stegs pa is the standard equivalent.
